items.question: How do you assess large language models as a path toward human-like intelligence?
items.object: Large language models as a path toward human-like intelligence
items.answer: First of all, I want to say there's nothing wrong with LLMs. LLMs are the basis for a lot of very useful AI products that all of us use, including me. They're great for what they do. items.question: Why do you see understanding the physical world as a harder AI problem than modeling language?
items.object: Understanding the physical world versus modeling language
items.answer: Language is very special in a way, and it's particularly well suited for the type of architectures that have been so successful recently, large language models, GPT-style architectures. But what about the real world? What about understanding the physical world? Reality is way more complicated than language because it's high-dimensional, continuous, noisy, and messy. Training a system to understand the real world is much, much harder. So that's really what we're after.

items.question: How do you distinguish exploratory AI research from the work of turning a promising result into products?
items.object: The transition from exploratory AI research to engineering and product development
items.answer: It's a strange trade-off. I see two modes of operating. There's a lot of exploratory research, a lot of research directions, and sometimes something seems to work and you need to push it further. It's not research anymore. The people working on it are still researchers, or they're called researchers in the press, but really it's becoming more engineering and pushing for products. That happened a number of times at Meta because of things that were started at FAIR, such as Llama. In early 2023, Llama 1, which was developed at FAIR, was very promising. Mark Zuckerberg was disappointed by it, rebooted the entire organization, reorganized it, and hired new people.

items.question: Why did you conclude that Meta was no longer the right place to develop your JEPA and world-model work into products?
items.object: Meta's suitability for developing JEPA and world models into products
items.answer: Over the last year, Meta realized they'd fallen behind a little bit, and that refocused the strategy on trying to catch up with the industry. The sad side effect is that exploratory research was not given high priority anymore. It didn't concern the stuff I was working on, all the JEPA and world models, because Mark himself, Bos, the CTO, and other people in the company were really interested in that project and believed in the long-term impact. We also realized that most of the applications were probably for things Meta was not particularly interested in. A lot of the applications are in industry, like manufacturing.

items.question: Why do you favor non-generative architectures over pixel prediction for learning representations of images and videos?
items.object: Non-generative architectures for learning image and video representations
items.answer:
I've been interested in learning models of the world by prediction for a very long time. I had an epiphany about five years ago, realizing that all the architectures that have been successful to learn representations of images and videos are non-generative architectures. All the generative ones basically have been failures. VAE, variational autoencoders, or autoencoders more generally, are a natural way to think about learning abstract representations of inputs. You put an image at the input of a neural net and train it to reproduce the input on its output. With a big neural net, if you just do it this way, your neural net will not do anything interesting; it will just learn the identity function. Completely uninteresting. It doesn't work. If you train a VAE to learn representations of images, you get something, but it's not that great. Same with sparse autoencoders.

Then you have another set of techniques, derivative of something called denoising autoencoder. Masked autoencoder is a version of this. BERT is a version for NLP. You take the image, corrupt it, and train the neural net to recover the original image. There was a huge project at FAIR on this called MAE, masked autoencoder. It was disappointing: a lot of computation, not a really satisfying result. Simultaneously, some of the same people working on MAE and others in Paris and New York were working on techniques using non-generative architecture, joint embedding architecture. Take an image, corrupt it, run the two images through encoders, and try to predict the representation of the original image from the representation of the corrupted one. That's JEPA.

JEPA means joint embedding predictive architecture. You have one encoder that makes an observation, another encoder that makes a different observation. You try to predict the representation of the first one from the second one with a predictor. Those techniques turned out to work much better for representing images and video. DINO V1, V2, V3, a project still going on at FAIR in Paris; I-JEPA and V-JEPA; before that SimSiam and MoCo and a bunch of different techniques, mostly from Meta, and others from other groups. That turned out to be a much better way of learning representations of images than predicting pixels.

items.question: How do you assess the progress shown by increasingly impressive robotics demos from model companies?
items.object: Robotics demos trained with imitation learning
items.answer:
I think there is real progress, and some of those demos are really impressive, but they are trained with enormous amounts of data collected either from teleoperation or from human action with things you hold in your hand that look like grippers. You collect the data for grippers, or track the hands and fingers of a person and translate this into commands for a robot. Those things are trained with imitation learning mostly, and a little bit with reinforcement learning to fine-tune, mostly in simulation.
The issue is that you need a lot of data to train the systems to imitate. It becomes expensive and a little brittle: you need to collect lots of data for every task you want the robot to solve. Whereas, if the system had a world model that allowed it to predict the outcome of an action, it would plan an action to solve a new task without having to be trained to accomplish this task. The degree of generalization with a world-model-based system would be much larger, a wider spectrum of tasks with less training data than a system trained with imitation learning and fine-tuning.

items.question: How do you assess synthetic training data as a route to autonomous driving that learns as quickly as a human teenager?
items.object: Synthetic training data and data efficiency in autonomous driving
items.answer: I'm sort of asking you again: why can a 17-year-old learn driving in 20 hours? You don't need millions of hours of demonstration, and you don't need synthetic data. You don't need any of that. I want a system that can learn as fast as that. If we crack that, then we don't need generated data. We might need to train the system in simulation, but not with the same amount of time or trials as current systems require. It's really a question of data efficiency.

items.question: Why do you see action-conditioned world models as a promising near-term application of AI?
items.object: Action-conditioned world models for complex industrial and biological systems
items.answer: Shorter term, there are many applications in industry where you need an intelligent system that can predict what's going to happen if I change this control variable on a complex system, be it a jet engine, a chemical plant, a power plant, a manufacturing line, a patient, a human cell. Those are systems sufficiently complex that you can't model their behavior with a small number of equations. The traditional way of modeling does not work. You need to train a neural net, a deep learning system, to model the dynamics of that system from data. What you get at the end is a phenomenological model of that process, of that system. If it's action-conditioned, then you get a world model of that system that allows you to control it optimally for whatever purpose you have. I think the number of applications of this in industry is mind-boggling.

items.question: Why do you think people need a wide diversity of AI assistants rather than relying on assistants built by US and Chinese companies?
items.object: AI assistant diversity and sovereignty
items.answer:
It's an idea I've been forming over the last three years or so: people increasingly use AI assistants for various things. You see a decrease in the use of general traditional search engines, and you just ask a question to your favorite AI assistant. If the plan Meta and others are developing of having smart devices like smart glasses is realized, you'd just be talking to your AI assistant by voice with your smart glasses or maybe some other smart device. All of your information diet will be mediated by AI assistants.
If you're somewhere in the world outside the US or China and you have an AI assistant built in California or Beijing, Shanghai, or Shenzhen, it's not good for you. You may speak a language those systems haven't been trained to handle particularly well. You may have a culture not well understood by people in Silicon Valley and China, not well represented by training data publicly available on the internet. You may have a value system not represented by people building those models. You'll almost certainly have political opinions not represented by the handful of AI assistants you might be able to get from West Coast tech companies or Chinese companies.
What's the solution? How do you serve a farmer in India, or even a philosopher in France or Germany? You need a platform which is an open, free foundation model, LLM-style, fine-tunable by anyone to cater to the interests of people speaking a particular language, having a particular culture, value systems, political biases, creeds, whatever it is. You need a wide diversity of AI assistants. A lot of countries that are neither the US nor China want some level of sovereignty for AI, not just for their industry, but also for their citizens. They don't want their citizens brainwashed by a Chinese model or a Canadian model, actually.

items.question: How do you envision Tapestry reconciling a globally trained frontier AI model with countries' desire for AI sovereignty?
items.object: Tapestry's proposed open, federated foundation model
items.answer:
The way you get an open platform like this to the frontier is you train it on more and higher-quality data than the proprietary systems. People in India, France, Vietnam, Morocco, Switzerland, Korea, Japan, Kazakhstan, everyone wants sovereignty. They tell you they've been training their model locally. They don't have to share their data. That's the crucial aspect of Tapestry. You would have international contributors contributing to training a global model that would constitute a repository of all the world's knowledge and culture. Contributors would contribute data and computing resources, but preserve control of their data. They would not have to share their data with other contributors. What they would contribute is parameter vectors.
It would be a federated-learning-style thing where you have a bunch of data centers. They get the parameter vector from the global consensus of a model. Think of it as an average of all the parameter vectors of all the contributors. All contributors periodically tell everyone else through maybe a central server, "Here is my parameter vector. What is yours?" You exchange parameter vectors like this. A local worker, whenever it updates its parameter vector, also tries to make it as close as possible to the global consensus vector. As the training progresses, all those parameter vectors converge toward a consensus model, essentially a repository of all human knowledge.
Now you have an open model as good as if it had been trained on all the data in the world, and you can fine-tune it for your own purpose, your own political, cultural, and linguistic biases, whatever you want or centers of interest. I think there is a natural force for this to happen because most countries that are not the US or China want sovereignty, but also because AI is fast becoming a platform, and there's a natural tendency for platforms to become open. items.question: How do you understand the significance of LLMs' success in mathematics and programming?
items.object: LLMs' strengths and limitations in mathematics and programming
items.answer:
I think the important point is that LLMs are particularly successful at domains where the language itself is the substrate of reasoning. Think about those two domains, mathematics and code. Those are domains where the language itself is the substrate of reasoning. It's not the only substrate, but when you do mathematics in the formal way on a piece of paper, not the intuitive stuff, you manipulate language. LLMs are really good at this. Proving theorems and things like that is what LLMs are really good at. They're not so good at coming up with good concepts and definitions. It's more like, here's a problem, solve it. They're problem solvers. Mathematics is not just problem solving; most of it is a creative act that those things don't do.
Same for code. LLMs are good programmers. They're not software architects; they're not computer scientists, but they can program for us. They can help us build things. Humans go one level up in the abstraction hierarchy; our world is to decide what to build. Building it, you can get help from LLMs. The important point is that LLMs are particularly successful at domains where the language itself is the substrate of reasoning, not for anything else.

items.question: How do you understand Geoffrey Hinton's change of view on AI after GPT-4 came out in 2023?
items.object: Geoffrey Hinton's change of view on AI after GPT-4
items.answer:
I didn't change my mind. They changed their mind. About the same time, it was basically GPT-4. Geoff was not connected to any of that. He was never really interested in LLMs and discovered GPT-4 in 2023 when it came out. He had an epiphany and said, "Oh my God, those systems are really close to human-level intelligence and possibly they have subjective experience." He did a quick calculation: the human cortex has about 16 billion neurons. If you want to do something like backprop—the brain doesn't do backprop directly, but if it does something like backprop, some sort of gradient estimation for some sort of objective function—you'd probably need a network of a few neurons to reproduce the functionality of a virtual neuron in a neural net. Let's assume maybe you need a circuit of ten actual neurons to reproduce what a backprop neuron does. Then your cortex is only 1.6 billion neurons. Oh my God, GPT-4 is really close to this. Maybe it's going to get as smart as humans.

I do not believe in this claim at all. This is Geoff's way of saying, "Okay, basically I can retire. I can declare victory. I searched for the learning algorithm of the cortex all my career. Maybe I didn't discover what it really was, but backprop seems to be a good substitute for it. It works really well. Maybe that's all we need, so I can retire and go around the world and give talks about the potential promises and dangers of AI." That's what I think his intellectual trajectory has been. He's much less vocal about the potential dangers now than he was a year or two ago. He realized there's probably a way to design truly intelligent systems. First, he realized current LLMs are not that smart. Second, there is probably a need for a few breakthroughs, conceptual breakthroughs, before we get to human-like intelligence. Third, the blueprint of those systems will be quite different from LLMs, and we probably have a way of making them controllable. I've been saying this for years, but he discovered this recently.

items.question: How do you assess the safety of current LLM agents given their ability to complete long coding tasks?
items.object: Reliability and safety of current LLM agents
items.answer: Coding is something where you can verify that the code you generate satisfies your specification. But not everything is coding. There are examples of coding agents wiping up your hard drive or doing stupid things that make you lose a lot of money or data. I think LLMs in their current forms are intrinsically unsafe because they cannot predict the consequences of their actions, and because the way the task they accomplish is determined is subject to their training. You give them a prompt, and then they accomplish a task that corresponds to that prompt only to the extent their training has conditioned them to do the right task corresponding to the prompt. There is no hardwired constraint that will force them to accomplish this task and predict that the task will be accomplished properly.

items.question: Why do you see objective-driven AI as a safer foundation for agentic systems than current LLMs?
items.object: Objective-driven AI as a safer architecture for agentic systems
items.answer:
LLMs are intrinsically unsafe. I don't think there's any way to fix that in the current paradigm. What I've been proposing is the architecture I've been talking about: objective-driven AI. You give an AI system an objective: accomplish this task. How does the system know it will accomplish this task? It has a world model and predicts the outcome of a sequence of actions it imagines taking. If this outcome satisfies a cost function that describes to what extent the task has been accomplished, then that system, if it works by optimization, finding a sequence of actions that accomplishes the task and minimizes this cost according to its world model, can do nothing else.

Of course, many things can go wrong. The cost function might be inaccurate; it might not accurately measure to what extent the task has been accomplished. The world model might be inaccurate, so the system's prediction is not the right one. It can still make mistakes, but it can predict the consequences of its actions to some extent, which is indispensable for any agentic system. You can add not just a cost function that guarantees a task has been accomplished, but other objective functions or costs, or even safety constraints: "Don't hurt anybody on the way." You can have low-level objective functions that put together will guarantee the system will not be dangerous, and the system cannot violate those things by construction. It will have to satisfy those conditions. That's not the case for an LLM. The LLM can always escape. There's a gap between your training error and test error. There's always going to be a prompt where the system does really stupid things.

items.question: How do you think a research lab should turn breakthrough ideas into practical innovations?

items.answer: I think a culture of openness and scientific process is necessary for breakthrough innovation. There's a whole chain of innovation: blue-sky research, new concepts, a lot of that in universities, some in advanced research labs in industry, which can be counted on the fingers of one hand. items.question: Why did you conclude that Meta was no longer the right environment for developing JEPA world models?

items.answer: Mark Zuckerberg read that paper, knew what it was about, and subscribed to the project. There was a lot of support in the leadership for this project we internally called AMI. It started really working for video. But then the company refocused all its effort on LLMs. Despite support from Mark and Andrew Bosworth, all the layers below didn't see the point, I think, so politically it became a little difficult. items.question: Why did you argue for open-sourcing Llama 2?

items.question: How has the development of self-supervised learning compared with what you originally hoped it would achieve?
items.object: The development of self-supervised learning
items.answer:
The whole idea of what we used to call unsupervised learning, which we now call self-supervised learning. Until about 2003, the whole idea of unsupervised pre-training, where you get a good representation for the input data and then either fine-tune the model with a little bit of supervised labeled data. It gave us some evidence that this whole technique could work. I tried to apply this to video because ultimately what I wanted to do was train a system to understand how the world works by just watching the world go by. That's the basic idea. I started to argue for this in the early 2010s. We did some work on simple video prediction; we didn't have GPUs. Then, after the creation of FAIR, we did this more seriously by doing pixel-level video prediction and realizing that wasn't working, but arguing for self-supervised learning: training a system generically, not to solve a task, but to predict, and then using the representation learned this way as input to a downstream task that you can train supervised or with reinforcement learning.

That was the topic of the second half of my keynote at NeurIPS in 2016. It was still called NIPS at the time. I kept pushing for this idea and tried to discover methods to get it to work. What surprised me is that it became incredibly successful, but not for video—for language. LLMs are a blindingly successful example of self-supervised learning.

items.question: Why do you see prediction about the real world as a different problem from next-token prediction in an LLM?
items.object: Language-model prediction versus representation prediction for the real world
items.answer:
Let me tell you one thing. An LLM works because when you have a sequence of discrete symbols, making predictions is easy. There are only a finite number of possible symbols in your language, 100,000 possible tokens or something like that. Your neural net can produce a probability distribution over all possible tokens, then you can sample from that distribution, shift the token into the input, and produce the next token. You can do autoregressive prediction. That's a special case.
If you have the real world, you can't use a generative model. You have to train a system that learns a representation and makes prediction in the representation space. There's a big issue with this, which I didn't think until about five years ago was easily solvable, even though I invented one technique to solve it decades before that. If you take two inputs, the initial segment of a video and the continuation, or one image and a corrupted version, run them both through an encoder, and train a predictor to predict the representation of one from the representation of the other, there's a very simple solution where the system predicts a constant representation and the prediction problem becomes trivial. That's called collapse, representation collapse. The big question of self-supervised learning for JEPA, for the joint embedding architecture, is how do you prevent collapse?

items.question: How do you assess contrastive learning and distillation as ways of preventing representation collapse in joint embedding architectures?
items.object: Contrastive learning and distillation as methods for preventing representation collapse
items.answer:
The solution I came up with many years ago, in 1993, is contrastive learning. You have examples of things that should be predictable from one another, and examples of things that should not be predictable from one another. This method works, but it doesn't scale with dimension; it doesn't scale very well.
Now you have the JEPA architecture. You have to come up with a good way of preventing collapse. There are a couple ways. As I said, contrastive methods are not a good approach. There are distillation methods, and they prevent collapse. We don't know why. A good example is DINO. It's a joint embedding method using distillation: one encoder trains the other, used as a teacher. For the encoder being trained, you do backprop. For the one not being trained, you don't do backprop, but share the weight with the other one with an exponential moving average. It's a collection recipe. There was a paper from DeepMind called BYOL, Bootstrap Your Own Latent, which uses this trick. That trick is derived from intuition from reinforcement learning. Somehow it prevents collapse, but we don't know why. There are a few theoretical papers explaining why it might work in simple cases, but it's not satisfactory. The cost function you think you're minimizing, you're not actually minimizing, so you can't monitor it. It actually goes up when you train. It makes sense. We don't like this method, but it works. Some models we've trained, large-scale video representation learning systems V-JEPA, V-JEPA 2, V-JEPA 2.1, train using this method. I-JEPA also.

items.question: Why are you enthusiastic about SigReg as a direction for training world models?
items.object: Information-based regularization, SigReg, and Le World Model
items.answer:
We're moving away from this, and now we have a few papers that came out recently on a specific regularizer to prevent collapse, which tries to maximize the information content coming out of the encoder. It's in the same family as Becker and Hinton from '89 and Schmidhuber in 1992, and others since then, and to some extent contrastive techniques too, although it's not simple contrastive. The question is how do you measure information content? How do you maximize the information content coming out of a neural net? If you want to maximize the quantity, you either need to measure it or have a lower bound on it. Information content, we only have upper bounds. We cannot measure it; we can only come up with upper bounds. So we take an upper bound and cross our fingers. It kind of works.
The latest one is called SigReg, sketch as isotropic Gaussian regularization. We had a previous one called VCReg, or VICReg, variance invariance covariance regularization. The SigReg stuff is really cool. This is work by Randall Balestriero, who was a postdoc with me and is an assistant professor at Brown now. It consists in forcing the distribution of variables coming out of the encoder to be joint Gaussian, essentially, maximizing information if you want. It's a very different way of doing it from what Jürgen Schmidhuber and Subbarao and Jeff Hinton were doing.
This is super promising, in my opinion, and we have variations of it that can produce sparse representations, another that can produce anisotropic representations but not necessarily Gaussians. We have a paper with Randall and a student at Mila, Luca Mice, where we train a world model with this. It's still small scale, but we think it's super promising. If you want to read one paper, read that paper. It's Le World Model, L-E World Model.
